claim: Wss1 is a SUMO-binding protein.
source: Hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged Wss1 and mutants were expressed in bacteria and their interaction with SUMO-beads was analyzed (Figure 1B). The beads bound HA-Wss1, suggesting a direct interaction with SUMO.
evidence: Demonstrated by pull-down experiments showing HA-Wss1 binding to SUMO beads (Figure 1B).

claim: Mutation of the conserved H and E residues of the WLM active site (WLM*) did not affect SUMO binding.
source: Mutation of the conserved H and E residues of the WLM active site (WLM*) did not affect binding, but deletion of SIM2 (ΔSIM2), mutations in SIM1 (SIM1*), or both (SIM1*; ΔSIM2) resulted in a significant decrease in binding.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO-bead binding assays with Wss1 mutants (Figure 1B).

claim: Deletion of SIM2 (ΔSIM2), mutations in SIM1 (SIM1*), or both (SIM1*; ΔSIM2) resulted in a significant decrease in SUMO binding.
source: Mutation of the conserved H and E residues of the WLM active site (WLM*) did not affect binding, but deletion of SIM2 (ΔSIM2), mutations in SIM1 (SIM1*), or both (SIM1*; ΔSIM2) resulted in a significant decrease in binding.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO-bead binding assays with Wss1 mutants (Figure 1B).

claim: Complete inhibition of Wss1 binding to SUMO was only achieved by triple mutation (SIM1*; ΔSIM2, WLM*).
source: Complete inhibition of Wss1 binding to SUMO was only achieved by triple mutation (SIM1*; ΔSIM2, WLM*) suggesting that all these elements are involved in the interaction with SUMO.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO-bead binding assays with Wss1 mutants (Figure 1B).

claim: Both N-terminal (Wss1 1–188, containing WLM and SHP) and C-terminal (Wss1 189–269, bearing the VIM and SIMs) fragments of Wss1 were retrieved on SUMO beads.
source: This was further confirmed by the observation that both N-terminal (Wss1 1–188, containing WLM and SHP) and C-terminal (Wss1 189–269, bearing the VIM and SIMs) fragments of Wss1 were retrieved on SUMO beads.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO-bead binding assays with Wss1 fragments (Figure 1B).

claim: The interaction of Wss1 with SUMO was specific because it was inhibited by free SUMO in solution and not by Ub.
source: The interaction was specific because it was inhibited by free SUMO in solution and not by Ub.
evidence: Competition experiments showing inhibition by SUMO but not Ub (Figure 1B).

claim: Wss1 was reported to be Ub/SUMO isopeptidase.
source: Because Wss1 was reported to be Ub/SUMO isopeptidase (Mullen et al., 2010) and the WLM domain contributes to SUMO binding, we hypothesized that WLM might bind the carboxy-terminus of SUMO.
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Mullen et al., 2010).

claim: SUMO-PA beads retrieve significant amount of Wss1 protein.
source: Under these conditions no Wss1 was bound to SUMO, while SUMO-PA beads still retrieve significant amount of the protein.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO-PA bead binding assays (Figure 1C).

claim: The binding of Wss1 to SUMO-PA was inhibited by o-phenanthroline (OPA) and WLM* mutation.
source: Pointing to the role of Zn, the binding to SUMO-PA was inhibited by o-phenanthroline (OPA) and WLM* mutation, while ablation of SIMs had only a minor effect.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO-PA bead binding assays with inhibitors and mutants (Figure 1C).

claim: The WLM domain appears to bind the C-terminus of SUMO.
source: Thus, the WLM domain appears to bind the C-terminus of SUMO and introduction of the phosphonic acid moiety enhances this interaction.
evidence: Inferred from SUMO-PA binding experiments (Figure 1C).

claim: Introduction of the phosphonic acid moiety enhances the interaction of WLM domain with SUMO.
source: Thus, the WLM domain appears to bind the C-terminus of SUMO and introduction of the phosphonic acid moiety enhances this interaction.
evidence: Inferred from SUMO-PA binding experiments (Figure 1C).

claim: No Wss1 was retrieved with Ub-PA beads.
source: On the other hand, the phosphonic acid moiety alone was not sufficient to insure binding since no Wss1 was retrieved with Ub-PA beads (Figure 1C).
evidence: Experimental data from Ub-PA bead binding assays (Figure 1C).

claim: Wss1 preferentially binds HMW-SUMO chains.
source: Indeed amylose pull-down experiments with recombinant MBP-Wss1 demonstrated that Wss1 preferentially binds HMW-SUMO chains (Figure 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from amylose pull-down experiments (Figure 1D).

claim: Both SIM1* and ΔSIM2 mutation inhibit binding of SUMO chains by Wss1.
source: Both SIM1* and ΔSIM2 mutation inhibit binding of SUMO chains, whereas mutation in WLM domain has no effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO chain binding assays with Wss1 mutants (Figure 1D).

claim: Mutation in WLM domain has no effect on binding of SUMO chains by Wss1.
source: Both SIM1* and ΔSIM2 mutation inhibit binding of SUMO chains, whereas mutation in WLM domain has no effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO chain binding assays with Wss1 mutants (Figure 1D).

claim: Recombinant Wss1 lacks protease activity.
source: Recombinant Wss1 lacks protease activity (Stingele et al., 2014), possibly due to improper protein folding or a specific cofactor requirement.
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Stingele et al., 2014).

claim: GFP-Wss1 formed nuclear foci.
source: Because we observed that GFP-Wss1 formed nuclear foci (see below) and others have reported activation by DNA (Stingele et al., 2014), we examined whether Wss1 protease activity can be triggered by nucleic acids and other negatively charged macromolecules.
evidence: Observation from microscopy experiments (see below in manuscript).

claim: Others have reported activation of Wss1 by DNA.
source: Because we observed that GFP-Wss1 formed nuclear foci (see below) and others have reported activation by DNA (Stingele et al., 2014), we examined whether Wss1 protease activity can be triggered by nucleic acids and other negatively charged macromolecules.
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Stingele et al., 2014).

claim: Refolding of Wss1 in the presence of ssDNA induced autocatalytic cleavage of the Wss1 protein.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that refolding in the presence of ssDNA-induced autocatalytic cleavage of the Wss1 protein (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from protein refolding experiments (Figure 2A).

claim: Uncleaved Wss1 and one fragment (N-Wss1) precipitated along with the DNA while the other (C-Wss1) was soluble.
source: Uncleaved Wss1 and one fragment (N-Wss1) precipitated along with the DNA while the other (C-Wss1) was soluble.
evidence: Experimental observation from protein refolding experiments (Figure 2A).

claim: Sequencing of C-Wss1 revealed cleavage at V189.
source: Sequencing of the latter revealed cleavage at V189 (Figure 2A).
evidence: Protein sequencing data (Figure 2A).

claim: No cleavage was observed with the WLM* mutant suggesting an autoproteolytic mechanism.
source: No cleavage was observed with the WLM* mutant suggesting an autoproteolytic mechanism.
evidence: Experimental data from protein refolding experiments with WLM* mutant (Figure 2A).

claim: Nuclease S1 inhibited Wss1 processing.
source: As nuclease S1 inhibited Wss1 processing, the cleavage cofactor seems to be ssDNA polymer and not individual nucleotides.
evidence: Experimental data from protein refolding experiments with nuclease S1 (Figure 2A).

claim: The cleavage cofactor seems to be ssDNA polymer and not individual nucleotides.
source: As nuclease S1 inhibited Wss1 processing, the cleavage cofactor seems to be ssDNA polymer and not individual nucleotides.
evidence: Inferred from nuclease S1 inhibition experiments (Figure 2A).

claim: Addition of ssDNA to Wss1 resulted in measurable protein cleavage after 3 hr of incubation.
source: Addition of ssDNA to Wss1 resulted in measurable protein cleavage after 3 hr of incubation.
evidence: Experimental data from protein cleavage assays (Figure 2B).

claim: The cleavage of Wss1 by ssDNA was inhibited by OPA, suggesting metalloprotease activation.
source: This reaction was inhibited by OPA, suggesting metalloprotease activation.
evidence: Experimental data from protein cleavage assays with OPA (Figure 2B).

claim: The cleavage pattern of Wss1 was different from that previously observed with multiple bands around 17 kD and negligible amount of large N-Wss1 fragment.
source: Curiously, the cleavage pattern was different from that previously observed (Figure 2A) with multiple bands around 17 kD and negligible amount of large N-Wss1 fragment (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation from protein cleavage assays (Figure 2B).

claim: The pathways of Wss1 cleavage may differ depending on experimental conditions.
source: Thus, the pathways of Wss1 cleavage may differ depending on experimental conditions.
evidence: Inferred from differences in cleavage patterns under different conditions (Figure 2A, 2B).

claim: Treatment of Wss1 with OPA induced protein oligomerization.
source: During these experiments, we observed that the treatment of Wss1 with OPA induced protein oligomerization (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental observation from protein cleavage assays (Figure 2B).

claim: The oligomers are thiol-sensitive suggesting that they are disulfide linked.
source: The oligomers are thiol-sensitive suggesting that they are disulfide linked (see Figure 4D below).
evidence: Experimental data from thiol sensitivity assays (Figure 4D).

claim: In Wss1 protein, the active site Zn is linked to a cysteine residue, which is released by OPA and promotes the formation of intermolecular crosslinks.
source: We hypothesize that in Wss1 protein, the active site Zn is linked to a cysteine residue, which is released by OPA and promotes the formation of intermolecular crosslinks.
evidence: Hypothesis based on OPA-induced oligomerization and thiol sensitivity.

claim: Wss1 is regulated by a cysteine-switch mechanism.
source: This observation raises an interesting possibility that Wss1 is regulated by a cysteine-switch mechanism (Chakraborti et al., 2003).
evidence: Hypothesis based on OPA effects and literature on cysteine-switch mechanisms (Chakraborti et al., 2003).

claim: Thiram efficiently induces Wss1 self-cleavage.
source: By screening a panel of different electrophiles, we found that thiram (Balakirev and Zimmer, 1998), a compound that reversibly modifies cysteine residues, efficiently induces Wss1 self-cleavage (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data from protein cleavage assays with thiram (Figure 2B).

claim: The cleavage pattern of Wss1 by thiram was the same as in refolding experiments.
source: Importantly, the cleavage pattern was the same as in refolding experiments (Figure 2A).
evidence: Comparison of cleavage patterns (Figure 2A, 2B).

claim: Thiram belongs to the thiuram disulfide class of reactive compounds that modify protein sulfhydryl groups via thiol-disulfide exchange reaction.
source: Thiram belongs to the thiuram disulfide class of reactive compounds that modify protein sulfhydryl groups via thiol-disulfide exchange reaction (Neims et al., 1966; Vallari and Pietruszko, 1982) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Neims et al., 1966; Vallari and Pietruszko, 1982) and figure supplement.

claim: Thiram inhibited OPA-induced Wss1 oligomerization.
source: Because thiram also inhibited OPA-induced Wss1 oligomerization (Figure 2B), it seems that it targets the same cysteine residue that is involved in Zn binding.
evidence: Experimental data from protein oligomerization assays (Figure 2B).

claim: Thiram targets the same cysteine residue that is involved in Zn binding.
source: Because thiram also inhibited OPA-induced Wss1 oligomerization (Figure 2B), it seems that it targets the same cysteine residue that is involved in Zn binding.
evidence: Inferred from thiram inhibition of OPA-induced oligomerization (Figure 2B).

claim: APMA produces Wss1 self-cleavage and inhibits OPA-dependent protein oligomerization.
source: In parallel, we found that toxic organomercury compound APMA, classically used for matrix metalloproteases activation, also produces Wss1 self-cleavage and inhibits OPA-dependent protein oligomerization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Experimental data from protein cleavage and oligomerization assays with APMA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).

claim: DNA damage or a defective SUMO pathway triggers the activation of Wss1 metalloprotease resulting in Wss1 self-processing and degradation of associated proteins.
source: Altogether, these data demonstrate that DNA damage or a defective SUMO pathway triggers the activation of Wss1 metalloprotease resulting in Wss1 self-processing and degradation of associated proteins.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from multiple assays.

claim: Wss1 proteolysis in the cell is SUMO dependent.
source: Because Wss1 proteolysis in the cell is SUMO dependent, Wss1 acts as a SUMO-targeted metalloprotease.
evidence: Inferred from cellular experiments showing SUMO-dependent Wss1 proteolysis.

claim: Wss1 acts as a SUMO-targeted metalloprotease.
source: Because Wss1 proteolysis in the cell is SUMO dependent, Wss1 acts as a SUMO-targeted metalloprotease.
evidence: Inferred from cellular experiments showing SUMO-dependent Wss1 proteolysis.

claim: Addition of ssDNA to Wss1 resulted in measurable protein cleavage after 3 hr of incubation.
source: Addition of ssDNA to Wss1 resulted in measurable protein cleavage after 3 hr of incubation.
evidence: Experimental data from protein cleavage assays (Figure 2B).

claim: Thiram greatly accelerated DNA-dependent Wss1 self-cleavage.
source: While thiram greatly accelerated this reaction, thiols, particularly 10 mM glutathione, significantly inhibited DNA-induced Wss1 proteolysis.
evidence: Experimental data from protein cleavage assays with thiram and thiols (Figure 2D).

claim: Thiols, particularly 10 mM glutathione, significantly inhibited DNA-induced Wss1 proteolysis.
source: While thiram greatly accelerated this reaction, thiols, particularly 10 mM glutathione, significantly inhibited DNA-induced Wss1 proteolysis.
evidence: Experimental data from protein cleavage assays with thiols (Figure 2D).

claim: In cells, spontaneous activation of Wss1 by DNA may be inhibited by intracellular/nuclear thiols.
source: This result implies that, in cells, spontaneous activation of Wss1 by DNA may be inhibited by intracellular/nuclear thiols.
evidence: Inferred from thiol inhibition of DNA-induced Wss1 proteolysis (Figure 2D).

claim: Oxidative damage would be expected to deplete thiols and increase ssDNA lesions, resulting in activation of the latent protease activity of Wss1.
source: Conversely, oxidative damage would be expected to deplete thiols and increase ssDNA lesions, resulting in activation of the latent protease activity of Wss1.
evidence: Logical inference from thiol inhibition and DNA activation of Wss1.

claim: Wss1 was reported to be a SUMO isopeptidase.
source: Because it has been reported that Wss1 is a SUMO isopeptidase (Mullen et al., 2010) and we observed that it binds specifically polysumoylated substrates (Figure 1D), we examined whether it disassembles SUMO chains.
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Mullen et al., 2010).

claim: Wss1 binds specifically polysumoylated substrates.
source: Because it has been reported that Wss1 is a SUMO isopeptidase (Mullen et al., 2010) and we observed that it binds specifically polysumoylated substrates (Figure 1D), we examined whether it disassembles SUMO chains.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO chain binding assays (Figure 1D).

claim: Wss1 treatment did not result in accumulation of low molecular weight SUMO species expected from chain disassembly.
source: While there was a reduction in the apparent molecular weight of the chains, we did not observe accumulation of low molecular weight SUMO species expected from chain disassembly and seen with Ulp1.
evidence: Experimental observation from SUMO chain processing assays (Figure 3).

claim: Wss1 failed to cleave a SUMO1-FP isopeptide substrate.
source: Also, in contrast to Ulp1, Wss1 failed to cleave a SUMO1-FP isopeptide substrate (Geurink et al., 2012) and was unable to process a linear His6-Ub-SUMO-HA substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Wss1 is not an isopeptidase.
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO1-FP cleavage assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Wss1 was unable to process a linear His6-Ub-SUMO-HA substrate.
source: Also, in contrast to Ulp1, Wss1 failed to cleave a SUMO1-FP isopeptide substrate (Geurink et al., 2012) and was unable to process a linear His6-Ub-SUMO-HA substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Wss1 is not an isopeptidase.
evidence: Experimental data from His6-Ub-SUMO-HA processing assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Wss1 is not an isopeptidase.
source: Also, in contrast to Ulp1, Wss1 failed to cleave a SUMO1-FP isopeptide substrate (Geurink et al., 2012) and was unable to process a linear His6-Ub-SUMO-HA substrate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), suggesting that Wss1 is not an isopeptidase.
evidence: Inferred from failure to cleave SUMO substrates (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: Wss1 treatment increases the intensity of high molecular weight SUMO able to penetrate the separating gel.
source: Instead, we found that Wss1 treatment increases the intensity of high molecular weight SUMO able to penetrate the separating gel (Figure 3).
evidence: Experimental observation from SUMO chain processing assays (Figure 3).

claim: Wss1 proteolysis generated SUMO species that more easily entered the gel matrix.
source: Because this reaction coincided with auto-proteolysis of Wss1 and was suppressed by OPA, it was probably catalyzed by Wss1 metalloprotease activity. Thus, it is likely that Wss1 proteolysis generated SUMO species that more easily entered the gel matrix and produced an apparent increase in SUMO signal.
evidence: Inferred from correlation with Wss1 auto-proteolysis and OPA inhibition (Figure 3).

claim: SUMO chains accelerated thiram-induced Wss1 auto-proteolysis.
source: Interestingly, SUMO chains accelerated thiram-induced Wss1 auto-proteolysis (Figure 3, lane 2 and lane 6).
evidence: Experimental data from SUMO chain processing assays (Figure 3).

claim: HMW-SUMO stimulates Wss1 cleavage, perhaps by promoting Wss1 oligomerization.
source: Thus, similarly to DNA (Figure 2B) HMW-SUMO stimulates Wss1 cleavage, perhaps by promoting Wss1 oligomerization.
evidence: Inferred from acceleration of Wss1 auto-proteolysis by SUMO chains (Figure 3).

claim: Wss1 has been reported to trim Ub from STUbL substrates.
source: Wss1 has been reported to trim Ub from STUbL substrates (Mullen et al., 2010) so we asked if expression of Wss1 reduced the levels of ubiquitylated SUMO conjugates.
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Mullen et al., 2010).

claim: Expression of Wss1 reduced the amount of ubiquitylated SUMO species in the cell.
source: Indeed, expression of Wss1 reduced the amount of ubiquitylated SUMO species in the cell but this reduction was independent of its metalloprotease active site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from cellular assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The reduction of ubiquitylated SUMO species by Wss1 was independent of its metalloprotease active site.
source: Indeed, expression of Wss1 reduced the amount of ubiquitylated SUMO species in the cell but this reduction was independent of its metalloprotease active site (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from cellular assays with Wss1 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: The effect of Wss1 on levels of ubiquitylated SUMO conjugates could be due to competition with STUbL for binding of SUMOylated proteins.
source: This suggests that the effect of Wss1 on levels of ubiquitylated SUMO conjugates could be due to competition with STUbL for binding of SUMOylated proteins.
evidence: Inferred from independence of metalloprotease activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Wss1 promoted sumoylation of cellular proteins.
source: Surprisingly, we found that Wss1 promoted sumoylation of cellular proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data from cellular assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: Substoichiometric amounts of recombinant Wss1 catalyzed formation of SUMO chains in vitro.
source: This effect was reproduced in vitro, where substoichiometric amounts of recombinant Wss1 catalyzed formation of SUMO chains (Figure 4A).
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro sumoylation assays (Figure 4A).

claim: Recombinant Wss1 and the WLM* mutant auto-sumoylate.
source: In parallel, we observed that recombinant Wss1 and the WLM* mutant auto-sumoylate (Figure 4B).
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro sumoylation assays (Figure 4B).

claim: The E3-like ligase activity of Wss1 results from the juxtaposition of an E2∼SUMO thiol ester and an acceptor SUMO due to polyvalent SUMO binding by Wss1.
source: Because the reaction was SIM-dependent, it is likely that this E3-like ligase activity (Figure 4A,B) results from the juxtaposition of an E2∼SUMO thiol ester and an acceptor SUMO due to polyvalent SUMO binding by Wss1 (Merrill et al., 2010).
evidence: Inferred from SIM-dependence and literature on SUMO ligase mechanisms (Merrill et al., 2010).

claim: The WLM* mutant showed higher SUMO ligase activity compared to WT protein.
source: The WLM* mutant that is unable to bind Zn repeatedly showed higher SUMO ligase activity compared to WT protein.
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro sumoylation assays (Figure 4A,B).

claim: Increasing OPA concentration promotes sumoylation of WT-Wss1.
source: Increasing OPA concentration promotes sumoylation of WT-Wss1.
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro sumoylation assays with OPA (Figure 4C).

claim: OPA did not increase the sumoylation of the WLM* mutant.
source: This effect was not due to stimulation of SUMO E1–E2 enzymes because OPA did not increase the sumoylation of the WLM* mutant.
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro sumoylation assays with OPA and WLM* mutant (Figure 4C).

claim: At 3 mM OPA, WT, and WLM* formed a similar level of SUMO conjugates.
source: At 3 mM OPA, WT, and WLM* formed a similar level of SUMO conjugates (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Experimental data from in vitro sumoylation assays with OPA (Figure 4C,D).

claim: Extraction of Zn from metalloprotease active site promotes Wss1-dependent sumoylation.
source: It seems therefore that extraction of Zn from metalloprotease active site somehow promotes Wss1-dependent sumoylation.
evidence: Inferred from OPA effects on sumoylation (Figure 4C,D).

claim: OPA induces Wss1 oligomerization.
source: Although the mechanism of this effect is not completely clear, it could be explained by our finding that OPA induces Wss1 oligomerization (Figure 2B).
evidence: Experimental data from protein oligomerization assays (Figure 2B).

claim: Wss1 oligomers are disulfide linked.
source: The oligomers can be seen by non-reducing gel electrophoresis and disappear in the presence of dithiothreitol (DTT) suggesting that they are disulfide linked (Figure 4D).
evidence: Experimental data from gel electrophoresis with DTT (Figure 4D).

claim: In the absence of Zn the regulatory cysteine 226 induces intermolecular disulfide crosslinks, multiplication of SUMO-binding sites and increase in SUMO ligase activity.
source: These data suggest that in the absence of Zn the regulatory cysteine 226 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) induces intermolecular disulfide crosslinks, multiplication of SUMO-binding sites and increase in SUMO ligase activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from OPA-induced oligomerization and increased sumoylation (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Wss1 is a SUMO-targeted minigluzincin-like metalloprotease that is regulated by a cysteine-switch mechanism.
source: In summary, our structural and biochemical analysis suggest that Wss1 is a SUMO-targeted minigluzincin-like metalloprotease that is regulated by a cysteine-switch mechanism.
evidence: Summary of structural and biochemical findings.

claim: In its latent form, Wss1 binds and promotes SUMO chain elongation.
source: In its latent form, Wss1 binds and promotes SUMO chain elongation, while upon activation by DNA binding the enzyme self-cleaves and is capable of processing HMW-SUMO.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on Wss1 activities.

claim: Upon activation by DNA binding the enzyme self-cleaves and is capable of processing HMW-SUMO.
source: In its latent form, Wss1 binds and promotes SUMO chain elongation, while upon activation by DNA binding the enzyme self-cleaves and is capable of processing HMW-SUMO.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on Wss1 activities.

claim: Wss1 may function by synthesizing and/or binding and processing polysumoylated substrates.
source: Thus, Wss1 may function by synthesizing and/or binding and processing polysumoylated substrates.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on Wss1 activities.

claim: Wss1 (chromosomally tagged with C-terminal Myc13) was immunoprecipitated from a cell lysate and bound partners were identified by mass spectrometry.
source: Wss1 (chromosomally tagged with C-terminal Myc13) was immunoprecipitated from a cell lysate and bound partners (Figure 5A) were identified by mass spectrometry (MS).
evidence: Experimental data from immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry (Figure 5A).

claim: More than 50 proteins were connected in a network with STRING and classified using the gene ontology (GO) database.
source: More than 50 proteins were connected in a network with STRING and classified using the gene ontology (GO) database (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis of mass spectrometry data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1).

claim: The majority of binding partners belong to nucleic acid metabolic pathways involved in DNA repair and regulation of RNA polymerase.
source: Consistent with the involvement of Wss1 in DDR (O'Neill, 2004), the majority of binding partners belong to nucleic acid metabolic pathways involved in DNA repair and regulation of RNA polymerase.
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis of mass spectrometry data and citation to previous literature (O'Neill, 2004).

claim: A third of the hits were proteins implicated in intracellular transport and membrane associated processes.
source: Surprisingly however, a third of the hits, many highly rated, were proteins implicated in intracellular transport and membrane associated processes.
evidence: Bioinformatics analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: The two most abundant Wss1 interactors were Doa1 and Cdc48.
source: The two most abundant Wss1 interactors were Doa1 and Cdc48.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data (Figure 5A).

claim: Wss1 interactions with Doa1 and Cdc48 were further confirmed by immunoprecipitation of HA-Wss1 from DOA1-FLAG cell lysates.
source: These interactions were further confirmed by immunoprecipitation of HA-Wss1 from DOA1-FLAG cell lysates (Figure 5B).
evidence: Experimental data from immunoprecipitation assays (Figure 5B).

claim: Doa1 is a Cdc48 cofactor that binds the C-terminus of the chaperone through its PUL domain.
source: Doa1 is a Cdc48 cofactor that binds the C-terminus of the chaperone through its PUL domain (Mullally et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Mullally et al., 2006).

claim: Both Cdc48 binding motifs of Wss1, SHP, and VIM, should interact with the N-terminal domain of Cdc48.
source: Because both Cdc48 binding motifs of Wss1, SHP, and VIM, should interact with the N-terminal domain of Cdc48 (Yeung et al., 2008; Hanzelmann and Schindelin, 2011; Stapf et al., 2011), we asked whether Wss1, Doa1, and Cdc48 form a ternary complex.
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Yeung et al., 2008; Hanzelmann and Schindelin, 2011; Stapf et al., 2011).

claim: Wss1 can bind Cdc48 and Doa1 separately.
source: Using purified recombinant proteins, we found that (i) Wss1 can bind Cdc48 and Doa1 separately (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), (ii) the proteins form a ternary 1:1:1 Wss1/Doa1/Cdc48 complex (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), and (iii) binding of Wss1 to Doa1 is specific, with few other Cdc48 cofactors observed in the pull-downs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays with purified proteins (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B).

claim: The proteins form a ternary 1:1:1 Wss1/Doa1/Cdc48 complex.
source: Using purified recombinant proteins, we found that (i) Wss1 can bind Cdc48 and Doa1 separately (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), (ii) the proteins form a ternary 1:1:1 Wss1/Doa1/Cdc48 complex (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), and (iii) binding of Wss1 to Doa1 is specific, with few other Cdc48 cofactors observed in the pull-downs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays with purified proteins (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).

claim: Binding of Wss1 to Doa1 is specific, with few other Cdc48 cofactors observed in the pull-downs.
source: Using purified recombinant proteins, we found that (i) Wss1 can bind Cdc48 and Doa1 separately (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), (ii) the proteins form a ternary 1:1:1 Wss1/Doa1/Cdc48 complex (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), and (iii) binding of Wss1 to Doa1 is specific, with few other Cdc48 cofactors observed in the pull-downs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays with purified proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C).

claim: The N-terminus of Wss1 binds the PFU domain of Doa1.
source: The results show that the N-terminus of Wss1 binds the PFU domain of Doa1, while the SHP and VIM motifs of Wss1 interact with the N-terminus of Cdc48 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down experiments with purified protein domains (Figure 5D).

claim: The SHP and VIM motifs of Wss1 interact with the N-terminus of Cdc48.
source: The results show that the N-terminus of Wss1 binds the PFU domain of Doa1, while the SHP and VIM motifs of Wss1 interact with the N-terminus of Cdc48 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down experiments with purified protein domains (Figure 5D).

claim: The NMR structure of the Wss1 VIM motif was determined.
source: Finally, we determined the NMR structure of the Wss1 VIM motif and used molecular docking and structure-based mutagenesis to identify R218, R219, F152 as key residues involved in Cdc48 binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: NMR structural data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: R218, R219, F152 are key residues involved in Cdc48 binding.
source: Finally, we determined the NMR structure of the Wss1 VIM motif and used molecular docking and structure-based mutagenesis to identify R218, R219, F152 as key residues involved in Cdc48 binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Molecular docking and structure-based mutagenesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: Mutation of all three of these residues (F2R) ablates Cdc48 binding.
source: Mutation of all three of these residues (F2R) ablates Cdc48 binding (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Experimental data from pull-down assays with F2R mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D).

claim: Doa1 confers Ub specificity to Cdc48 complexes.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that Doa1 confers Ub specificity to Cdc48 complexes (Mullally et al., 2006).
evidence: Citation to previous literature (Mullally et al., 2006).
